sections.h2: How is North Carolina organized, and who do I call about my house?
sections.html:
North Carolina has 100 counties, and almost everything that touches a house sale runs through the county where the property sits. Wake County is the most populous, Mecklenburg is second, and Dare is the largest by land area while Clay is the smallest.

Three county offices matter most to a seller.

  • The tax office, which bills and collects property tax and tells you what is owed before closing.
  • The register of deeds, which records the deed and collects the state excise tax when the deed is filed.
  • The clerk of superior court, who handles probate and foreclosure hearings.

The county list further down links to our recording and property tax guides. If your county has no guide, call its tax office and register of deeds.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work when I sell in North Carolina?
sections.html:
Property tax is set and collected locally, on a yearly cycle that starts January 1. Ownership of real property is fixed as of that date, and the bill is due September 1 of the fiscal year it covers. Pay before January 6 and no interest is added. After that, interest runs at 2 percent for the first stretch, then three quarters of a percent for each month or part of a month from February 1 until the bill is paid.

Values are not reset every year. The default is a reappraisal at least every eight years, and a county can choose a shorter cycle. Larger counties can be pushed to reappraise sooner if their assessments drift too far from sale prices.

Older owners and owners with disabilities may qualify for a break. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or half of the home's appraised value from taxation, for owners who meet the age or disability test and an income limit that changes each year. Applications are accepted through June 1 before the tax year. Our homestead guide and property tax guide walk through the steps, and the county tax office has the current income figure.

Unpaid bills are settled from the sale proceeds, so request a payoff figure from the tax office early.

sections.h2: What does recording cost, and who pays the deed tax?
sections.html:
The seller pays North Carolina's excise tax on deeds, and the register of deeds collects it before the deed is recorded. The rate is $1 for each $500 of value, or any part of $500.

ItemWhat the sources say
Deed excise tax$1 per $500 of value, paid by the seller at recording
Property tax due dateSeptember 1, interest free through January 5
Reappraisal cycleEvery eight years by default, shorter if the county chooses
Elderly or disabled exclusionGreater of $25,000 or 50 percent of appraised value
Debtor residence exemptionUp to $35,000 of equity in a residence
Executor application fee$120 for letters from the clerk
Foreclosure upset bid10 days, at least 5 percent more and not less than $750 above the last bid

Recording fees vary by county, so ask the register of deeds. Our excise tax page and closing cost page cover the seller side in more detail.

sections.h2: Who handles a North Carolina closing?
sections.html:
Expect an attorney. The State Bar's advisory opinion says most closing work is legal work, such as preparing deeds and examining title, and that a nonlawyer doing it without direct supervision by a North Carolina lawyer is practicing law without authority. Nonlawyers may present documents, direct signers and handle funds, but the legal steps belong to a lawyer, and the lawyer must be chosen by the party the lawyer serves. The Real Estate Commission urges clients to hire an attorney too.

In practice that means the title search, deed preparation and payoff of your mortgage or tax bills all run through a closing attorney's office.

A cash sale as-is means the buyer takes the property in its current condition and is not waiting on a lender. That can shorten the closing, but title work and recording still take the steps above.

sections.h2: What do I have to tell a buyer about the house?
sections.html:
Most sellers must give the buyer a residential property disclosure statement. On it you either answer the listed questions from your actual knowledge or check the box saying you make no representations about the condition of the property. Topics on the form include water and sewer, the roof and structure, plumbing, electrical and heating, wood-destroying insects, zoning issues, and environmental items such as radon, lead paint and asbestos. If you decline to make representations, you have no duty to disclose that item, even if you should have known about it.

Several transfers are exempt from the disclosure rule entirely:

  • Transfers by a personal representative or other fiduciary administering an estate, guardianship or trust
  • Foreclosure sales and other court-ordered transfers
  • Transfers between spouses or to direct-line relatives
  • Transfers between co-owners
  • Transfers caused by unpaid taxes

Ask your attorney whether the fiduciary exemption fits your sale.

sections.h2: How does probate work for an inherited house in North Carolina?
sections.html:
The elected clerk of superior court in each county acts as the probate judge. The clerk issues letters testamentary when there is a will and letters of administration when there is not, and banks and insurers often ask to see them. The filing fee to apply for letters is $120.

Land and houses generally are not run through the estate unless the will says so or the house must be sold to pay debts. That varies with how title was held, so the next step is to read the deed and talk to an estate attorney. Property held with a right of survivorship passes outside probate. Our probate page lays out the general order of events.

Taxes keep accruing while the estate is open, so heirs who plan to sell often start with the tax office.

sections.h2: What happens in a North Carolina foreclosure?
sections.html:
North Carolina uses a power of sale process that goes through the clerk of superior court. The lender or trustee files a notice of hearing, and service must be made at least 10 days before the hearing. At the hearing the clerk checks that a valid debt exists, the borrower is in default, the loan documents allow foreclosure, and everyone entitled to notice received it. A finding can be appealed to a judge within 10 days.

If the clerk allows the sale, notice of it must be posted at least 20 days before the sale date and published once a week for two successive weeks in a local legal newspaper. After the auction, anyone can raise the bid within 10 days. The new bid has to beat the last one by at least 5 percent and at least $750, backed by a deposit. Each raise opens another 10 day window.

Tenants have some protection. For residential property with fewer than 15 rental units, the sale notice must say that tenants on rentals signed or renewed after October 1, 2007 can end the lease with written notice taking effect 10 to 90 days after the sale.

Owners who are behind should call the lender and an attorney early. Taxes work differently. A county can foreclose a tax lien through a court action modeled on a mortgage foreclosure, and the owner can redeem before the court confirms the sale by paying the taxes, interest and costs. See our tax lien and tax deed page for the background.

sections.h2: What if my house has tenants or needs work?
sections.html:
Read any lease before you list. For tenancies without a set end date, notice depends on the rental period.

  • Year to year: at least one month of notice, given before the year ends
  • Month to month: seven days
  • Week to week: two days
  • Manufactured home space: 60 days regardless of the period

A landlord can bring a summary ejectment case when the term has ended, when the tenant did something that ended the right to stay under the lease, or in a few other listed cases, after demand for possession. Utility arrears alone cannot be the ground for ending a lease. Our eviction page and landlord and tenant page cover the court steps.

Condition problems in North Carolina often come from water. The state's floodplain mapping site, FRIS, publishes flood hazard data and maps, and after a storm the state health department tells owners not to use a flooded well or a submerged septic system until it has been checked. County health departments handle well permits, water testing questions and septic issues. The NC Radon Program recommends testing every home, including homes that already have a mitigation system, at least every five years. Keep any test and repair records you have.

faqs.q: How many counties does North Carolina have?
faqs.a: North Carolina has 100 counties. Most sale paperwork goes through the county where the house sits.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed excise tax when I sell?
faqs.a: The seller pays it to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded. The rate is $1 for each $500 of value.

faqs.q: When are North Carolina property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are due September 1. Taxes paid before January 6 carry no interest, and interest starts after that date.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to close a house sale?
faqs.a: In practice, yes. The State Bar says legal parts of a closing, such as title review and deed preparation, need a North Carolina attorney.

faqs.q: Who handles probate for an inherited house?
faqs.a: The clerk of superior court. Houses often pass outside the estate unless the will says otherwise or debts require a sale.

faqs.q: Do I have to give a buyer a disclosure form?
faqs.a: Usually, though you may state that you make no representations. Estate, foreclosure and family transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: How long does a North Carolina foreclosure take?
faqs.a: It varies. Hearing notice is served at least 10 days ahead, sale notice runs at least 20 days, and a 10 day upset bid period follows the auction.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Review the lease term and notice rules before you sell, and ask an attorney about your case.
